IV. Isotropic Quantum Dot Results

Although the main focus of this project was to develop a computational model for simulation, preliminary simulations have produced some promising results. Isotropic quantum dot growth results are presented in Figures 1-3. Figure 1 (a)-(c) show the evolution of stable quantum dots from a randomly perturbed this film. The coloring denotes the height of the film at each frame – red represents the highest points and purple the lowest. The simulation shows that dots form at random positions and at a variety of sizes.

Quantum dots have a characteristic spacing λ at which they prefer to grow. When perturbations were put in a film at even multiples of λ, a regular array of dots was produced (Fig. 2). The array of dots looks qualitatively similar to the self-assembled arrays of dots produced experimentally by depositing a SiGe film on a patterned Si(001) substrate.¹⁰ However, when perturbations were placed halfway between multiples of λ, a situation occurred where the growth of separate dots interfered with each other.

An interesting phenomenon discovered through the simulation and documented experimentally is the formation of a quantum ring structure (Fig. 3). Simulation of a small mound on a smooth surface produced a quantum ring (Fig. 3(b)) which has been observed by AFM in a CdTe/ZnTe system (Fig. 3(a)). Unlike the simulation in which interfacial energy is completely isotropic, the CdTe/ZnTe system has interfacial anisotropy present which produces some slight facets in the structure and causes the shape to differ slightly from the simulation.
V. Regularization of Anisotropic Interfacial Energy

Anisotropic interfacial energy was introduced into the phase-field model because some degree of interfacial energy anisotropy is found in may material systems. The interfaces arrange so that they minimize surface energy, possibly resulting in the formation of facets or cusps when interfacial anisotropy is present. Anisotropic crystal equilibrium shapes are found by generating an interfacial energy description in 3D and solving for the Wulff construction. The interfacial energy model does not correspond to any particular crystal structure (i.e. FCC, BCC, HCP), although it has been constrained to be four-fold symmetric. The anisotropic interfacial energy used in the 3D numerical simulation is defined by the following equation:
